content.thinking:
The user reports that their PC keeps crashing, and I’ve been gathering logs to pinpoint the cause. So far, the evidence shows that the most recent boot (boot -1) ended abruptly without a clean shutdown, suggesting a hard crash or power loss. Earlier boots also show similar abrupt endings: boot -4 ends with the same “Concurrent access to the ACPI EC detected” messages, and boot -1 has a series of errors but no graceful shutdown sequence. The pstore directory exists, but I haven’t inspected its contents yet; however, the pattern of sudden terminations points to a possible hardware or kernel panic event rather than a service failure.

The most recent logs I pulled (from the last 10 minutes before the crash) still show a flood of “Concurrent access to the ACPI EC detected” messages, which could indicate an ACPI-related race condition, but that alone doesn’t explain a full system freeze. I also observed that the CPU temperature is fairly high (78 °C) right now, which could be a factor if the system was under load before the crash. I need to know what was happening on the system just before the crash: which processes were consuming CPU, any spikes in load, and any other kernel messages that might have been logged in that critical window.

Therefore, the next logical step is to capture a snapshot of the current system state (uptime and top CPU consumers) and then examine the journal for the last few minutes of the previous boot, filtering out the repetitive ACPI EC race messages so they don’t drown out other potentially relevant entries. I’ll limit the journal query to the period from 19:10 on 2026‑06‑10 (the crash occurred around 19:21) and pull the last 30 lines after filtering. This should give me a concise view of what was happening right before the crash, while also letting me see if any particular user process or kernel driver was active.

Thus, I will run a Bash command that:
1. Calls `uptime` to see how long the system has been up (useful for correlating with the crash time).
2. Lists the top CPU‑using processes with `ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -8`.
3. Queries the journal for boot -1, limited to entries since 19:10, excludes the noisy ACPI EC lines, and shows the last 30 lines.

This combination directly addresses the unknowns: current load, recent activity, and any non‑ACPI messages that could hint at the crash cause. I’ll issue this as a tool call now.

arguments.command: uptime; ps aux --sort=-%cpu | head -8; echo ===; journalctl -b -1 --no-pager --since "2026-06-10 19:10" | grep -vE 'ACPI EC|Race condition' | tail -30
arguments.description: Check current load and last 10 min before crash
